articles.title: Suspected measles cases kill nearly 1,000 as Bangladesh struggles to contain outbreak
articles.summary: A measles outbreak sweeping across Bangladesh has killed hundreds of children following setbacks to the South Asian nation’s vaccine program.
articles.body: DHAKA, Bangladesh — Eight-month-old Rojatun Jannat Ramisa is struggling to breathe in a hospital in Bangladesh’s capital as her parents sit helplessly beside her. She is one of thousands of children sickened by a measles outbreak that is sweeping across the South Asian country and has killed hundreds of children following setbacks to the national vaccine program. Ramisa’s mother, Ranu Akhter, traveled hundreds of miles after doctors in eastern Bangladesh referred her to a specialized child hospital in Dhaka to seek treatment for the life-threatening condition. “Fourteen days ago, when we were at the district hospital, there were other children being treated alongside my daughter. I saw that those children also had red rashes on their bodies, sores in their mouths and fevers,” Akhter told The Associated Press at Dhaka Shishu Hospital. “It made me realize how widespread the measles outbreak is,” she said. Every day, the death toll is rising. Bangladesh has been racing to halt the outbreak’s spread since March, when more than 100 children died in less than a month. By Tuesday, the death toll from suspected measles cases reached 999 since the start of the year, according to the government’s Directorate General of Health Services. Since March, the country has recorded more than 166,000 suspected measles cases, including 19,835 laboratory-confirmed infections, according to the Ministry of Health. The government launched an emergency vaccination drive in March together with the World Health Organization, the U.N. children’s agency and the Gavi vaccine alliance. It began with a focus on children from 6 months to 5 years old and later expanded nationwide in phases. Measles is a highly contagious airborne disease that causes fever, respiratory symptoms and a characteristic rash. It can sometimes have severe or fatal complications, especially in young children, according to the WHO. Two doses of a vaccine provide strong protection against measles, but the WHO says 95% of the population has to be vaccinated in order to stop the disease from spreading — which protects children like Ramisa who are too young to be vaccinated as well as immunocompromised people. About 86% of children in Bangladesh got their recommended second dose of measles vaccine last year, according to an estimate by the World Health Organization and UNICEF. That’s down from 93% in 2024. A few years ago, Bangladesh had measles largely under control, with a vaccination program that was credited for decades for protecting children and mothers from the deadly diseases of tuberculosis, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, poliomyelitis and measles. From 2021 to 2025, the country recorded just 100 to 300 cases per year, down from 2,410 cases in 2020. But in the last few years, disruptions to the vaccine program have left a growing number of children unvaccinated. First the Covid-19 pandemic interrupted routine vaccinations, and then in 2024 the government largely missed a vaccination campaign previously carried out every four years. Atiqul Islam, a neonatal and child specialist at Bangladesh Shishu Hospital and Institute, said that during the pandemic period in 2021 and 2022, many parents did not take their children to get vaccinated. “So, if you look at children who are now 4 or 5 years old, many of them missed their vaccinations. That created a gap. During the previous interim government, vaccines were also unavailable at many vaccination centers,” he said. Bangladesh’s current government, headed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, said the failures in planning under ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and interim leader Muhammad Yunus left the country with shortages of vaccines and far behind on coverage. The 2024 measles vaccination campaign was disrupted during the political upheaval that led to Hasina’s ouster. She left the country in the face of a mass uprising in August 2024, and was followed by Yunus, who led an interim administration that transferred power to an elected government after an election in February. From exile in India, Hasina blamed the Yunus-led government for the disaster. At Bangladesh Shishu Hospital, Islam said the situation has improved, but not enough. The doctor said his colleagues are struggling to treat infected children who often arrive at the hospital with serious complications such as pneumonia, diarrhea and encephalitis, or brain swelling. “For the past six months, we have been treating measles patients continuously, and we are exhausted,” he said.

articles.title: Five dead and 86 missing as fire breaks out on ferry in the Philippines
articles.summary: The fire broke out as the vessel nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron in Palawan.
articles.body:
At least five people have died and 86 are missing after a fire broke out on a ferry in the Philippines, the country's coastguard said.

The MV June Aster, which set off from Manila ferrying 117 passengers and 17 crew members, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron when it caught fire.

The blaze, which erupted at 18:45 local time (10:45 GMT) Wednesday, was still burning as of 11:00 on Thursday. The strong currents and thick smoke were a challenge to those working to extinguish it, the coastguard said.

A survivor says he was in the sea for two hours before he got rescued. "It was cold. If the rescue was delayed, I would definitely have died," Roland Lerma told the BBC.

Video clips shared by the coastguard on Wednesday night showed the vessel engulfed in flames and people being pulled out of the water into rescue boats.

The cause of the fire remains under investigation, the coastguard said.

The coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest the fire started in the cargo hold, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, the coastguard said. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.

Forty-three people have been rescued but it is unclear how many have sustained injuries.

Seven of the survivors were taken to a hospital in Culion, a larger neighbouring island, which has higher bed capacity and more comprehensive healthcare services.

A first responder told the BBC they had never seen such a disaster in Coron, calling it "really heartbreaking".

"I was one of the people who carried and transported the casualties to the hospital last night," they said, adding that the ferry was an hour away from its destination.

The survivors were taken to an evacuation centre in Barangay Turda, which sits just north of Marcilla. The state of their injuries is unclear.

Anelyn Magbanua is among those anxiously waiting for news of their loved ones.

Her husband Marlon had spent a few days in Manila visiting their two children, who were going to school in the capital city.

Magbanua last heard from him while the ferry was passing through a village about two hours from the port in Coron, she tells the BBC.

"I was expecting that the ferry will arrive at the pier at between 18:00 and 19:00 yesterday," she said, adding that she had gone to bed early but was awakened by a cousin who told her the ferry Marlon was on had caught fire.

"I couldn't describe what I am feeling right now. I have been crying and praying since last night," Magbanua says.

She'd travelled to a hospital in Coron, hoping to find Marlon among the survivors – but he remains unaccounted for.

"My two-year-old son and I are outside the hospital as we speak. We have nothing but ourselves," she says.

Rai Garcia has three family friends among those missing.

Mae Lorraine Galera-Navoa, who is the sister of Garcia's brother-in-law, had travelled to Luzon to attend her father's funeral, accompanied by her husband Elyzer Navoa and their three-year-old daughter Hiraya Joy.

They had been travelling home to El Nido in Palawan on board the vessel when it caught fire.

"We haven't received any news yet. That's why we had to comment on local news threads just to receive updates," Garcia says.

"We still hope and pray for their safety."

Garcia and his family made a poster to appeal for information of the family of three using a photo Mae had taken on the ferry and shared with immediate relatives.

Others have posted on the Philippine Coast Guard's Facebook page asking for information of their missing loved ones. "Please can you find my sibling," read one comment.

Maritime accidents are common in the Philippines, an archipelago of 7,100 islands.

Inter-island ferries are a cheap way to move people and cargo between islands, some of which are inaccessible by air.

But there is always the risk of severe weather, monsoon rains and typhoons which can cause turbulent conditions. The country is affected by an average of 20 typhoons every year.

Past accidents have also been blamed on poor maintenance and uneven enforcement of safety laws.

In 2023, 31 people died after a fire broke out at a passenger ferry in the country's south-western tip. The MV Lady Mary Joy 3 was on its way to Basilan island from Zamboanga city, a major port in the main southern island of Mindanao.

But with 86 still missing, this ferry disaster could prove to be among the worst to have happened in the Philippines in recent years.

articles.title: Russia outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily use of new jet-powered drones
articles.summary: The new models can travel at speeds of up to 300mph, faster than Ukraine's air defence interceptors.
articles.body:
Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.

It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.

Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models.

"The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.

The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.

According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.

Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky . But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

Four Ukrainian companies have reportedly started testing missiles that can shoot down the new Geran models, officials in Kyiv recently told reporters. The country's new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has tasked them with producing "thousands of units" as quickly as possible.

Russia also had an economic incentive to invest in the jet-powered drones. The increased speed and manoeuvrability of these models means the line between them and more expensive cruise missiles has become "blurred", said John Hardie of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a think tank focused on national security and foreign policy.

"Long-range one-way attack drones are basically a poor man's cruise missile," he said. "The more you add capability to a drone, the less meaningful the distinction between the drone and a lower-end cruise missile."

But the analyst organisation Conflict Armament Research emphasised that jet-drones are not yet as advanced as cruise missiles. It said the munitions have a shorter attack range, carry much smaller warheads and are more susceptible to jamming systems.

Meanwhile, satellite images appear to show Moscow is redesigning key facilities dedicated to fighting the war in Ukraine to host jet-powered drones, with longer rails associated with the munitions visible at an entirely new base at Tsymbulova in the Oryol region.

Multiple launch sites appear to have been built at the facility, which is around 109 miles (175 km) from the Ukrainian border.

Since the facility became operational, Tsymbulova appears to have become a key centre for Russian drone attacks. Oryol region, where the Tsymbulova base is located, was not mentioned as a drone launch site in Air Force reports before September 2024, but by August 2026 it was named in almost every attack.

The proliferation of jet-powered drones comes as BBC Verify found that Russia is now striking Ukraine with complex attacks involving hundreds of drones and missiles about once a week.

The increase in the size of the strikes is being powered by Moscow's shift towards combining a "greater variety of munitions" - including jet-powered and decoy drones - with expensive ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to intercept, analyst Michael Bohnert of the RAND think tank told BBC Verify. Kyiv's data shows that Moscow is now using over 15 times more drones per attack than it was four years ago.

Bohnert added that the tactically complicated nature of the assaults, coupled with a global shortage of air defence systems capable of halting ballistic missiles partly caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran, has led to falling interception rates by Ukraine.

Ukraine's Air Force data showed a drop in interceptions of ballistic missiles up to the end of July. In August, Kyiv mostly stopped publishing the figures that would show its interception rate.

articles.title: Buy now or wait and hope? Families face gamble on heating oil
articles.summary: The price of heating oil has almost doubled in 12 months following the conflict in the Middle East.
articles.body:
As the summer draws to a close, families who rely on fuel oil to heat their homes are facing a dilemma.

The price has almost doubled over the past year, following the outbreak of conflict between the US and Iran.

It has left people wondering whether to buy now for the winter, or hold off in the hope that prices will fall – with the risk that they could rise again.

John Craggs, 73, from Wigtoft, near Boston, Lincolnshire, needs to fill his tank ahead of winter.

"Over the next few weeks I'll be monitoring the price to see if it goes down a little bit and then order the oil," he says.

But whatever they decide, he and his wife Libby, 80, are planning to limit their heating this winter because of the cost.

"We've both had health problems over the last few years and we should be keeping warm but its just too expensive," John Craggs adds.

"We will only have the heating on up to about 17 degrees in three of the rooms in the house, between about 3pm and 8pm, just to keep the cost down to be able to afford it."

About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil, typically in rural areas. This includes more than 40% of homes in some parts of Lincolnshire, including Wainfleet All Saints, Wragby, Roughton and Ludford, according to Census data.

Unlike gas and electricity customers, they are not covered by the energy price cap, leaving them more exposed to sudden increases. They also have to pay a lump sum in advance for their fuel, with domestic tanks typically holding between 1,000 and 2,000 litres.

On Wednesday, the average price was 97.05p per litre, according to the comparison website boilerjuice.com , which measures the cost for purchases of 1,000 litres.

That figure is up by 85% since 9 September 2025, when it stood at 52.8p, and while it has dropped significantly from a high of 134p in March, prices have been climbing again in recent weeks after renewed fighting between the US and Iran .

It means a household wanting to fill a 1,000-litre tank could be facing a bill of more than £970.

In March, the government announced a support package worth £53m for low-income families who use heating oil after prices surged due to the conflict in the Middle East.

The funding is distributed by local authorities, which set their own criteria for eligibility.

John Craggs says he inquired about help, but found he did not qualify.

The charity National Energy Action wants to see the price cap that covers gas and electricity extended to include all forms of energy, including heating oil.

It is also calling on the government to provide more help to households.

Matt Copeland, the group's interim director of policy, said: "I don't think the level of support really anticipated the length of time these high prices would go on for. It's really important that the government does look at that again in the budget and allocates more funding to help people to afford their heating.

"The government should also look at widening the criteria so the low-income households outside of the benefit system who are really struggling to afford their energy bills can access the support that they need."

A spokesperson for the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero said: "Energy is an everyday essential and needs to be affordable for everyone, which is why we have cut VAT on electricity bills to give families breathing space.

"This follows taking £150 in costs off bills earlier this year, and we will keep looking at what more we can do to protect households."

articles.title: Scientists and fishermen celebrate return of bluefin tuna
articles.summary: Marine biologists and fisherman reflect on the increasing numbers of bluefin tuna in UK waters.
articles.body:
Scientists and fishermen are working together to get a better understanding of the increasing number of Atlantic bluefin tuna in the UK's waters.

Ecology professor at the University of Exeter Dr Lucy Hawkes said the bluefin population had collapsed through overfishing by the mid-1960s but was now thriving.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) called the return "one of the most exciting developments in our fisheries for decades" and the Marine Management Organisation (MMO) has approved the highest ever quota and number of permits to fishermen to catch them.

Newlyn fisherman Andrew Pascoe said: "I don't see any reason why the permits can't double again in the next three or four years if the science is good and the management says we can catch more."

Hawkes said the bluefin population had collapsed by the mid-1960s because there had been "some really excessive takes, particularly of juvenile bluefin".

"Too many were being killed before they ever had a chance to reproduce," she said.

She worked on an international research project, Thunnus UK, which tagged tuna in a bid to better understand their ecology.

Hawkes said: "One of the reasons a partnership with the fishing industry is really vital is because those are people who are out on the water all the time looking at the tuna.

"The stories I hear from anglers and skippers in the South West is that the numbers of fish they're seeing are going up dramatically."

Fisherman Pascoe said: "Since we saw the first tuna returned to our waters about 14 years ago now, the numbers have risen double every year, and the last two or three years there's absolutely thousands of them out there and right the way up through the English Channel - not just off here."

This year, the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) increased the UK's annual quota for bluefin tuna from 63 tonnes in 2024 and 2025 to 230 tonnes for 2026, 2027 and 2028.

The MMO doubled the number of commercial licences it offered from 15 last year to 30 this year, and offered 145 permits to to recreational fishers in England in 2026 and six in Jersey.

Defra said UK commercial fishers could land 120 tonnes of bluefin tuna this year, worth an estimated £1.4m based on historic landing prices.

A further 26 tonnes have been made available for the commercial-scientific trial fisheries, worth about £300,000 based on historic landing prices, it added.

Andy Wills, the MMO's interim head of future fisheries, described this year's bluefin tuna season as "an important milestone in the development of this emerging fishery as it features more quota and more permits than ever before".

A Defra spokesperson also said it was a momentous time.

"The return of bluefin tuna to UK waters is one of the most exciting developments in our fisheries for decades, creating new opportunities for commercial fishers, recreational anglers and coastal communities across the UK," they said.

Fishermen across the South West and six in Jersey have been granted bluefin licences.

Pascoe said: "All successful licence holders have got 4,000kg [8,820lb] of bluefin tuna for the year, and that's equivalent to about 3,600kg [7,940lb] of landed weight."

He said the equipment required to convert to catching tuna included rods, reels, lures and ice bags.

"All that equipment runs up to about £7,000 or £8,000, but it's a viable fishery.

"If we catch the whole quota, you could be talking about £50,000 or £60,000 worth of income, so it's a good fishery."

Hawkes said the total quota for the whole of Europe was about 40,000 tonnes, "so we are a very small slice of the pie".

"It doesn't mean our pie shouldn't be ethical, done with the highest standards of welfare, and what we can do as scientists is provide the best evidence to help that to continue to go in the right direction," she added.

"We're losing traditional species farther north with climate change and we've got these sort of species coming behind, tuna not directly linked, but octopus and bream species coming through," he said.

"So we have to make sure that we get the management right of these new species because, if we don't, there's nothing else for us to catch."

Brixham fish merchant Ian Perkes said there was a cost to the larger tuna population.

He said: "Tuna eat about 20% of their body weight per day, so your average 200kg [440lb] tuna per week, well, you can imagine.

"It's an awful lot of fish that we're missing, the sardines, mackerel and herrings.

"If the tuna stay, of course it will increase the revenue for all - the fishermen, the fish merchants and the town.

"It's a shot in the arm for us, which is brilliant.

"I'm a firm believer they're here for feed, so all the time there's something for them to eat, I'm pretty sure they'll stay."

Emily Theobald, science and policy lead at the Cornish Fish Producers Organisation, said she thought there were a few reasons for the rising numbers of bluefin tuna.

She said: "We're in a warming phase and global warming is certainly contributing to the fish returning here after things like sardine and feed, which are also doing really well as a result of global warming, so it's probably a combination of conservation and environmental factors."

Pascoe said he thought along the same lines.

He said: "It's the highest regulated fishery I've ever taken part in and that's why the stock has recovered.

"The fish are coming our way again now, not directly linked to climate change, but the plankton shift with the climate change and the warming waters.

"This has meant that the bait fish has come, and the whole food chain has come through that, and the tuna is coming back to our waters because there's lots of food here for them now."

In August, a giant Atlantic bluefin tuna was landed off Whitby on the Yorkshire coast for the first time in about 60 years.

It weighed 338kg (745lb) and was 2.93m (9.6ft) long and the following day another was landed which weighed slightly less.

Hawke, a member of the University of Exeter team which has tagged six tuna off Whitby, said: "One of the fish we caught, we believe, is the largest bluefin that's ever been caught in British waters, including the 1920s, 30s, and 40s, which was the heyday of bluefin tuna fishing."

She said the Thunnus UK team had been tracking bluefin tuna in the Channel since 2018 and not one of the 165 fish tracked had ever gone into the North Sea.

She said: "These are exceptionally migratory bluefin.

"It's entirely possible that these fish are actually Canadians coming over for a little summer holiday in the UK.

"They could also be the same genetic population as the ones that are being caught down in the Channel off Falmouth and Plymouth.

"It could be that these are an older version of them, maybe they're bigger because they're older and there's no way for us to know the answer to that question without doing the sort of science that we are."

For the first time, fishers granted licences to catch bluefin tuna must complete a training course run by the Angling Trust.

A spokesperson for the trust said: "Fishing for bluefin tuna is unlike anything else currently encountered in our waters.

"It is a large, powerful, highly mobile fish, and handling one safely, for the fish and for the people on board, takes specific skills."

The training, an online course and an in-person day, covered a syllabus which taught fish welfare, handling, equipment choices, revival and release technique, data recording and avoiding disturbance to other marine life, organisers said.

The spokesperson said: "We have a fantastic fishery on our doorstep that a decade ago was unimaginable, and it has become a valuable source of income for charter businesses and the coastal communities around them.

"We want that to continue and to equip everyone taking part with the knowledge to fish responsibly."

articles.title: BBC East celebrates 70 years of broadcasting from Norwich
articles.summary: The BBC set up its first East of England regional service in a converted Georgian mansion in 1956.
articles.body:
As the BBC spread across the UK in the 1920s and 30s, one part of the country remained conspicuously absent from its map – East Anglia.

Although the BBC transmitted national services to the region, they had no studio there until September 1956. That month, they opened a radio operation in a Georgian mansion in Norwich.

St Catherine's Close was the main base of BBC East until 2003, when services moved to Norwich's new Forum development.

On a Secret Norfolk episode , current BBC Look East presenter Susie Fowler-Watt said the old building had been a "beautiful place" that had "felt special" to work in.

TV and radio historian Paul Kerensa runs the British Broadcasting Century podcast , telling the story of the BBC's early years.

He says one of the reasons the BBC overlooked the East of England for so long is because they initially concentrated on opening studios in major population centres.

"If you didn't have a big city near you, you'd need a more powerful radio set to pick up many of the programmes – and a lot of patience till your area was covered."

The announcement in 1954 that the BBC was coming to Norwich made front page news in the local papers, with the studios eventually opening on 10 September 1956.

St Catherine's Close was reported at the time to have been one of the oldest buildings ever converted for broadcasting.

The BBC fitted many of the rooms with reproduction 18th Century furniture, and even some with genuine antiques.

There was a garden, a greenhouse, and a groundskeeper's cottage. Most of these gradually disappeared through the building's time as a BBC office, but the entrance hall's curved staircase and chandelier remained throughout.

Initially, staff produced radio programmes and news bulletins for the local frequency of the BBC Home Service – what is now BBC Radio 4.

The editorial area covered was roughly Norfolk, Suffolk, most of Cambridgeshire, and northern Essex.

BBC Local Radio did not launch until 1967, in Leicester, and there were no stations in the East of England until BBC Radio Norfolk opened in 1980.

Paul Kerensa says the threat of new commercial regional television services is likely to have been one of the reasons why the BBC finally decided to open a regional HQ.

"Technical advancements helped regional growth, and the threat of ITV accelerated the BBC's plans," he said.

In 1959, a small television studio was hurriedly added to St Catherine's Close so the BBC could beat the new ITV company Anglia Television to air with a regional TV news service.

At first, this was a 10-minute bulletin. The very first one on 5 October 1959 was given a special introduction live in the studio by Hugh Carleton Greene, who was due to become the next director-general of the BBC.

Read by local teacher and part-time broadcaster Geoffrey Harvey, that first bulletin included:

film of Prime Minister Harold Macmillan campaigning in Norfolk and Suffolk ahead of the impending general election

a report on Norwich shoe manufacturers exhibiting at London Shoe Week

footage of a new trawler at Lowestoft and a motorcycle event attended by 25,000 people at Shrubland Park near Ipswich

brief stories on fires in Norfolk and Cambridgeshire, a road accident in Ipswich, and a planning dispute in Norwich

football updates with team news on Norwich City and Ipswich Town

In 1962, the TV news from St Catherine's Close became a longer news magazine programme.

In 1964, this programme was renamed Look East . It is still broadcast from Norwich, now from a studio at The Forum.

Fowler-Watt joined the staff at St Catherine's Close in the late 1990s. She said it "felt almost like we were working in [someone's] home".

She said the BBC had "outgrown" it by the time they left in 2003 , but it was emotional when she and co-presenter Stewart White closed the doors on the building at the end of the final Look East to be transmitted from there.

"There was a real sense of loss in the same way of moving from a beloved family house. There's a history and so many memories tied up in that building."

articles.title: World's tallest living horse based in Towcester 'still growing'
articles.summary: Hugo the shire horse enters the record books as the world's tallest living horse.
articles.body:
A Shire horse that has entered the record books as the world's tallest living horse could exceed his height as he is still growing, his owner has said.

Hugo, who lives in Towcester, Northamptonshire, has already reached an "abnormal" 199cm tall, about 6.5ft to the withers or ridge at the base of the neck.

Guinness World Records said the four-year-old's stature was officially assessed by a vet and he was measured without shoes to ensure an accurate result.

Owner Brett Masters said Hugo received "a huge amount of care" from a chiropractor, dentist, vet and masseuse, meaning he lived a "five-star lifestyle".

Shire horses are known for their height and their large stature means they are able to pull heavy weight, which is why they have been historically used as working horses on farms and for transport.

The tallest and heaviest horse ever documented was a Shire gelding named Sampson, who was later renamed Mammoth - bred by Thomas Cleaver of Toddington Mills in Bedfordshire, which stood at 2.19 metres - or 7ft 2.5 in - in 1850.

Masters, from Tove Valley Shire Horses, said the breed was his passion.

He was approached by officials from Guinness World Records as Hugo was "locally famous", and they had been told: "There is this really big horse, you need to speak to these guys."

Masters said that when he acquired Hugo - at the age of 18 months - he had no idea he was "very tall, abnormally tall".

"He's still got three years of growing left, he won't stop until he's about eight and a half, he's only a baby," he said.

"It will cause issues, so we have to be very careful with him.

"He has a chiropractor, has regular massages, the dentist visits every six months, and the vet checks him all the time as his growing plates are hyperactive.

"He has lots of supplements and a careful feed regime.

"He lives a five-star lifestyle, he wants for nothing."

Masters added: "Every time he goes out, people stop, they film him, shout at you that 'he's massive'.

"He's the kindest, most gentle kind of horse."

He said he did not receive any form of payment for his official recognition, but joked: "If any carrot farmer wants to give him some carrots, he'd kindly have them."

Hugo is kept busy by taking part in demonstrations and showing people what shire horses would have done "back in the day, by pulling agricultural implements, driving wagons", and is now learning to have people ride him.

"He's very happy, and he just loves a good fuss," Masters added.

articles.title: Billy Boston funeral to take place
articles.summary: The funeral of rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston will take place in Wigan later.
articles.body:
The funeral of rugby league legend Sir Billy Boston will take place later.

Boston, who was the first player in rugby league's 130-year history to receive a knighthood, died last month aged 92.

His funeral will take place at Wigan Warriors' Brick Community Stadium at 12:30 BST, with a limited number of supporters able to attend.

Before the service, a cortege will travel through Wigan and arrive at the stadium. The West Stand will be open as Sir Billy makes his final journey through the Stadium Tunnel. A private burial will follow.

At the request of the Boston family, people attending are being encouraged to wear traditional funeral attire, but items of Wigan Warriors' cherry red can be worn such as scarves, ties and headwear.

People are welcome to pay their respects to the funeral cortege, which will follow a route through Wigan.

Born in Cardiff in 1934, Boston grew up playing union but was overlooked by his home club. He came to the attention of rugby league scouts while on national service in the north of England, signing for Wigan in 1953 as a 19-year-old.

He was picked for the 1954 Great Britain side and was the first black British player to tour Australia and New Zealand.

He reached the 100-try milestone in just 68 matches and claimed 478 tries in 488 games for Wigan, helping them win three Challenge Cups and the Championship.

In all, Boston scored 571 tries in his career - a total surpassed only by Australian legend Brian Bevan in top-class rugby league - and is one of the truly great British rugby league players.

articles.title: Europe’s far right: Putin’s best friend?
articles.summary: Its gains threaten to deepen Europe’s divisions over Ukraine and Russia.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin had a good week. It kicked off with the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, an opportunity to rub shoulders with international heavyweights such as Xi Jinping and Narendra Modi. Then, on Saturday, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff turned up in Moscow, signalling their boss – United States President Donald Trump’s – continued resolve to cut a deal on Ukraine with Putin.

But it was news from Europe that possibly brought the greatest joy to the Kremlin. Alternative for Germany (AfD)’s resounding success in the Saxony-Anhalt election brought the prospect of a Russia-friendly party running a regional government in a core European Union member state. For someone like Putin, who has a special relationship with Germany courtesy of his years as a KGB officer in Dresden, this surely feels satisfying.

AfD could see itself winning power at the federal level the next time voters head to the polls in 2029. Currently, the far-right party is on a roll, buoyed by dissatisfaction with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and its promises to clamp down on immigration, curtail LGBTQ rights, and roll back the transition to renewable energy. Its appeal is particularly strong in former East Germany, having already come first in the 2024 provincial elections in Thuringia.

Nationally, AfD polls six to seven percentage points ahead of the governing Christian Democratic Union (CDU). Unless the CDU bounces back, defying the odds, the populist hardliners would have the largest caucus in the next Bundestag. Should that happen, mainstream parties might struggle to uphold the much-talked-about firewall (Brandmauer) keeping AfD, whose ranks include neo-Nazis, out of office. Saxony-Anhalt, otherwise a small province with limited impact on national politics, could prove a testing ground for a coalition headed by the far right.

Russia could provide at least some of the glue for such a partnership. AfD is courting potential support on the left, for example, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), a splinter from the Die Linke party (heir to East Germany’s communists). Similar to the far right, Sahra Wagenknecht is arguing for cutting military aid to Ukraine, peace negotiations with Russia, and lifting EU sanctions. Their views on migration and gender issues are in sync too, and in fact, they resonate with Putin’s criticism of Europe going woke. So, if the AfD and BSW (or an equivalent force on the left) gain power in Berlin, they will opt for policies reminiscent of Viktor Orban’s Hungary. But Germany’s pivotal role in European politics, economy and security raises the stakes.

Though Germany may be grabbing headlines these days, the main concern is France. While Merz and the CDU have a longer time horizon, President Emmanuel Macron is on the way out. Marine Le Pen might well turn out to be the winner in the 2027 presidential election. Current polls suggest she might be able to beat a mainstream candidate.

A nationalist and Eurosceptic in the Elysee would no doubt complicate Europe’s pursuit of a more unified foreign policy in response to external challenges, with Russia at the top of the list. Unlike the AfD, Le Pen’s National Rally (RN) favours some military aid for Ukraine, though not at the current scale. However, they call for negotiations and lambast the EU for what they describe as a misguided effort to defeat Russia. With Le Pen in charge, EU enlargement, whether to the Western Balkans, Ukraine or Moldova, would be put in the freezer. Admitting new members has already been made tough by the French constitution requiring a supermajority in the two chambers of the legislature or a national referendum. If Europe gives aspiring countries the cold shoulder, Russia will win, by default rather than design.

The latter highlights a key point. It is tempting to blame the rise of illiberal parties and politicians on Moscow’s machinations, in the same way that many Democrats in the US painted Trump’s win in 2016 as a result of Russian meddling. Yet, while it is beyond doubt that populists and nativists share views aligned with the Kremlin, their popularity with voters has to do with their ability to exploit genuine economic grievances and cultural anxieties.

What Russia’s influence campaigns usually do is to amplify social cleavages and feed resentment in order to disrupt the established order from within. But the choice, as well as the responsibility it entails, lies squarely with the voters in a given democracy, be it France, Germany, the US, Greece (where a Russia-friendly coalition of the far right and far left won power in 2015), or anywhere else.

One should also bear in mind that hardliners’ policies and views evolve, especially when they get elected. That has been the case with Giorgia Meloni in Italy, who had become a staunch backer of Ukraine and Western unity by the time her Brothers of Italy won in 2022. In the same vein, RN has moved to the centre on many issues, including EU integration and Russia policy, under Le Pen and her deputy Jordan Bardella.

Thus far, AfD has been the exception. It sticks to its extreme positions and, all things considered, the strategy works for it. But in the longer term, the party might have to tack to the centre in order to attract disgruntled CDU voters, particularly outside its East German turf, and persuade others to dismantle the Brandmauer. Radicalism might eventually run its course.

Saxony-Anhalt happens to be the part of Germany where Catherine the Great’s family hailed from. Putin, amateur historian that he is, might well remember that. Having his ideological allies run the place is not quite the conquest worthy of Catherine. But it is a point for Moscow, which is already putting pressure on Germany through reckless acts of sabotage such as the drone attack foiled at Leipzig airport. The populist revolt across Europe need not lead to radical change in a direction Russia wants. Yet it will create enough disruption inside the EU to hobble its intermittent effort to assume a greater geopolitical role.

articles.title: India launches trafficking investigation after five baby orangutans found abandoned in forest
articles.summary: Orangutans are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia
articles.body:
Five baby orangutans, not native to India, were found in a forest in Odisha, prompting an investigation into possible trafficking by an international smuggling network.

The young orangutans, between one and two years old, were given first aid and taken to a zoo in Bhubaneswar for health checks and quarantine.

Orangutans are classified as critically endangered, and despite protections under Cites and Indian wildlife law, they continue to be trafficked for private collectors and as exotic pets.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in the Indian state of Odisha , thousands of kilometres from their natural habitat, prompting an investigation into how they got there.

Orangutans are not native to India. They are found in the wild only in Indonesia and Malaysia, and all three recognised species – Bornean, Sumatran and Tapanuli – are classified as "critically endangered" by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

Odisha's forest minister said investigators were examining whether the animals had been trafficked by an international smuggling network and abandoned near a highway.

His government had asked India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau to investigate, the minister said, adding that local police, forest officials and a special task force were involved in the inquiry.

The apes were found on Tuesday in Ranakata, a proposed reserve forest in Bhogarai block, district forest officer Pratik Prakash Indalkar said. They were spotted close to a state highway by villagers.

The animals could not have reached Odisha naturally and might have been transported there by road, Mr Indalkar said. "The area is covered mainly by casuarina trees and isn't a dense forest," he said. "It's also close to a state highway."

The police's special task force is revisiting old orangutan smuggling cases to establish whether an organised trafficking network is involved.

"We are analysing similar cases and contacting teams that looked into them," deputy inspector general of police KV Singh told the Indian Express .

"We are currently gathering data and carrying out local inquiries."

Forest officials said they believed the orangutans had been in the area for only two to three days before they were spotted. A search of the surrounding forest found no other orangutans or clues as to how the animals had arrived, Mr Indalkar said.

Officials described them as infants, though some local reports suggested they were between one and two years old.

Their young age raised particular concern, wildlife expert Biswajit Mohanty said. Young orangutans typically remain with their mothers for several years while they learn to survive independently, and females usually give birth only once every eight years, making it unusual for five young animals to be found together with no adults nearby.

The animals, three males and two females, were given first aid before being taken to the Nandankanan Zoological Park in the capital Bhubaneswar, where they underwent health checks and were placed in a quarantine facility.

"Three animal keepers and a special veterinary team have been assigned to take care of them and we are also monitoring them through CCTV," Pradeep Mirase, the zoo's deputy director, told the Express .

"As one of them had a fever, authorities administered medication. They are stable now. Our focus is to stabilise them, following which we would conduct some tests."

A special diet chart has been drawn up in consultation with the Mysore Zoo, which is home to three orangutans and has experience caring for the species.

The animals are being fed every two hours, with the youngest given mashed potatoes and apples, and the others bananas and apples, alongside milk.

Zoo officials have also provided toys and slings to the animals, who have appeared to enjoy staying together as a group.

Commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites, the global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife, and they are also protected under Indian wildlife law. Despite this, orangutans continue to be trafficked to private collectors and for sale as exotic pets.

The native habitat of orangutans has also been under severe pressure of late.

Wildfires in Indonesian Kalimantan, on Borneo, affected about 60 per cent of Bornean orangutan habitat between June and August this year, according to an analysis by the environmental group Geopix, which recorded some 18,000 fire hotspots inside the orangutan habitat during that period.

The group said the fires were worsened by the climate crisis and a strong El Nino.

Conservationists in the region separately reported rescuing orangutans directly threatened by the fires in recent weeks, including a mother and baby moved to a rescue centre in West Kalimantan after flames spread close to their habitat.

This is not the first time young orangutans have been found in India. In 2022, two baby orangutans were discovered abandoned at a checkpoint near the border between the states of Assam and Mizoram, with officials suspecting they had been brought into the country through neighbouring Myanmar.

articles.title: “It’s not about taking credit”: MP youth, 'Bittu Tabahi', who cleaned a garbage-filled river responds to Dhruv Rathee’s ‘PR’ and 'photoshoot' remark
articles.summary: Surendra Singh Choudhary, aka Bittu Tabahi, did something unthinkable and became a national hero. The 21-year old, a BSc student from Biaora in Madhya.
articles.body: Surendra Singh Choudhary, aka Bittu Tabahi, did something unthinkable and became a national hero. The 21-year old, a BSc student from Biaora in Madhya Pradesh, himself stepped into the polluted Ajnar River and started the cleaning work. The river was suffering from heavy pollution and was full of plastic bottles, weeds and other waste. Bittu pulled out all the garbage with his own hands, without any help from a large clean-up team or heavy machinery. Online, he got the name ‘Bittu Tabahi’ for his remarkable work.His efforts eventually took him from the banks of a garbage-filled river to a meeting with Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav in Bhopal. While the world praised his efforts and he also received a job offer from an established firm, his meeting has now triggered a new conversation after YouTuber Dhruv Rathee accused the government of trying to take credit for Bittu’s work.But Bittu did not agree with Rathee’s words and politely responded to his remarksHis response was simple: “It’s not about taking credit. It’s about civic sense.”Bittu’s months-long missionBittu started his river-cleaning work on January 26, 2026. At that time the Ajnar River was in an extremely bad situation from continuous pollution. This was bothering him for some time, particularly the plastic, bottles, algae and other waste that had accumulated in and around the water body.But Bittu did not complain, he decided to start cleaning.As per reports he initially started the work with some friends, but the effort eventually became largely his own. He continued returning to the river and removing waste on his own. His before-and-after visuals and videos began circulating widely on social media. He often worked without proper protective equipment, handling waste and polluted material directly. Because of this, he contracted skin infections but his determination was beyond any medical condition.His story therefore became more than a simple before-and-after clean-up video.Then came the CM meetingAs Bittu's story went viral, it reached the Madhya Pradesh government. Chief Minister Mohan Yadav called him to his residence and met him and his family in Bhopal. He publicly praised his determination.Yadav highlighted his initiative as an example of how meaningful change can begin with one person. The chief minister also assured him of government support for his efforts. A video of their interaction was subsequently shared on the CM's social media account.For Bittu, the meeting was recognition of work that had already been going on for months.Dhruv Rathee calls it a ‘PR’ stunt and photoshootReacting to the video of Bittu's meeting with the chief minister, YouTuber Dhruv Rathee questioned why the government had stepped in after the young man's work became viral.In a comment reported by multiple publications, Rathee wrote: “Aa gaye credit lene.. Sara kaam ek ladke ne kiya aur jab viral hua toh use bula liya photoshoot ke liye…” He went on to question what the government was doing and alleged that it was “sirf PR” — public relations.The criticism centred on one question: if Bittu had been cleaning the river for months, why did official recognition come only after his work became a social-media talking point?It was a question that could easily have turned into another online political argument. However, Bittu's response took the conversation to the real issue.Bittu's turned it into the real question: ‘The issue here is civic sense’Bittu directly responded to Rathee“Dhruv Bhaiya credit lene ki baat nahi hai, Govt. ne pehle bhi mere kaam ko appreciate kia hai,” he wrote. He then explained what he believed the real issue was: “Baat yaha civic sense ki hai.”Bittu said he wanted people to understand their own responsibility and come forward for cleanliness, just as he had.That response is perhaps the most interesting part of the entire episode.Bittu's argument clearly states that it’s not the responsibility of the government alone to keep the environment clean. Nor is he saying citizens can simply ignore civic authorities. His point is that keeping a river clean cannot end with one clean-up drive if people continue throwing waste into it.The problem is here of Civic SenseEven after portions of the Ajnar were cleaned, reports noted that people had begun dumping waste again. The problem, therefore, is bigger than removing garbage once. It involves changing the behaviour that puts the garbage there in the first place.A river can be cleaned by one determined person. Keeping it clean requires many more.His efforts have also attracted recognition from the ace industrialist Anand Mahindra. Boyan Slat, founder and CEO of Netherlands-based The Ocean Cleanup, reportedly offered Bittu an opportunity to work with the organisation impressed by his work.And after becoming famous for cleaning it, he is asking people not to wait until another person has to clean it again and understand their responsibilities.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.title: 30 Kansas inmates donate $4,267 from their own funds to pay down local children's lunch debt
articles.summary: US News: Nearly 30 incarcerated men in northwest Kansas have donated $4,267 to help pay down unpaid school meal debt at Norton Community Schools, turning money.
articles.body: Nearly 30 incarcerated men in northwest Kansas have donated $4,267 to help pay down unpaid school meal debt at Norton Community Schools, turning money raised inside a correctional facility into support for children in their local community. Members of Reaching Out From Within, a rehabilitation programme at Norton Correctional Facility, raised $3,810 from their personal funds during a spring and summer fundraiser. Kansas Department of Corrections staff added another $457, bringing the total to $4,267. The donation was presented to Norton Community Schools Superintendent Corey Roy on August 3 and will help provide meals for children whose families have struggled to pay their school accounts.Kansas inmates raise $4,267 from their own fundsThe fundraiser began after members of Reaching Out From Within learned that Norton Community Schools, USD 211, had accumulated about $6,000 in unsettled meal debt by the end of the 2025-26 school year. The debt had built up from breakfast and lunch served to students whose families were facing food insecurity and could not pay their children's accounts. Rather than simply discussing the problem, members of the prison-based programme decided to organise a fundraiser. They eventually collected $3,810 from their own personal funds, while Kansas Department of Corrections staff contributed another $457. The resulting $4,267 donation covered roughly 71% of the reported $6,000 debt.Donation was presented to school superintendentThe money was formally presented during a ceremony at Norton Correctional Facility on August 3, when nearly 30 incarcerated men gathered to hand the donation to Norton Community Schools Superintendent Corey Roy. The facility said the money was intended to be "paid forward" and used to help local children fuel their day and remain focused and energised during the school year. Roy said he was moved by the men's desire to make a positive impact on other people in their community. He also spoke with participants individually and as a group, telling them that their actions had made a positive difference.Reaching Out From Within focuses on rehabilitationThe donation came through Reaching Out From Within, or ROFW, an incarcerated-led rehabilitation programme established in Kansas in 1982. According to the organisation, its purpose is to help incarcerated people make lasting changes in their behaviour, become role models for nonviolence and eventually return to their communities as contributing members. ROFW says its groups now operate in all 15 adult correctional facilities in Kansas, as well as facilities in North Carolina and a transition centre in Kansas City, Missouri. The programme uses regular meetings and peer support to encourage participants to examine destructive behaviour, develop healthier relationships and prepare for life after incarceration.Many participants understood the struggle with hungerThe lunch-debt fundraiser also carried a personal connection for some of the men involved. Organisers said many participants had grown up in financially unstable households and remembered experiencing hunger themselves. That background gave the men a direct understanding of why a school meal can matter to a child whose family is struggling financially. The fundraiser therefore allowed participants to help children facing a problem that some of them had experienced earlier in their own lives. At the same time, the available reporting does not establish that every participant personally experienced childhood hunger, so that detail is best attributed to the organisers rather than applied to all of the men.Donation highlights both kindness and a wider problemThe $4,267 contribution does not completely erase the district's reported $6,000 meal debt, but it substantially reduces it and provides direct assistance to families struggling with food costs. The episode has also prompted a broader conversation about food insecurity and the circumstances that allow school meal debt to accumulate in the first place. At the same time, the donation offers a striking example of the kind of community contribution that rehabilitation programmes such as ROFW seek to encourage. Men serving time at a Kansas correctional facility chose to use their own funds to help children outside its walls, turning a local financial problem into an opportunity for service and positive change.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hong Kong court convicts Wall Street Journal publisher of deterring reporter from taking union role
articles.summary: A Hong Kong court on Thursday convicted the publisher of The Wall Street Journal of deterring its reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city.
articles.body: HONG KONG — A Hong Kong court on Thursday convicted the publisher of The Wall Street Journal of deterring its reporter from taking up a trade union role, in a case that raised concerns about press freedom in the city. The court acquitted Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia) Inc. of the charge of dismissal over the union role. Former WSJ reporter Selina Cheng, also chairperson of the trade union Hong Kong Journalists Association, launched a private prosecution against Dow Jones Publishing Co. (Asia) Inc. after losing her job in July 2024. Hong Kong, a Chinese territory once considered a bastion of press freedom in Asia, has seen its media landscape change drastically in recent years, including the forced closure of news outlets and the prosecution of newsroom leaders. Principal Magistrate David Cheung convicted the defendant of the first charge but said the defense had raised sufficient reasonable doubt for the second charge. Cheng earlier said her supervisor told her that her participation in the union election was problematic and that the supervisor needed to discuss the issue with the Journal management in New York and Dow Jones’ in-house lawyers. Cheng said she was told that her union role would be incompatible with her employment. Dow Jones pleaded not guilty last year to two charges under the city’s Employment Ordinance, each carrying a maximum fine of 100,000 Hong Kong dollars (about $12,750). The first charge alleges the company had prevented or deterred Cheng from exercising union participation rights. The second alleges the company terminated her employment for exercising those rights. During the trial, the defense tried to convince the court that Cheng was terminated because of redundancy and argued the prosecution had not sufficiently proved that the Journal’s management instructed Cheng’s supervisor. The defense also accused Cheng of acting in bad faith in a previous hearing. Sentencing is expected to be handed down at a later date. Cheng’s termination in 2024 alarmed many journalists, especially given that foreign outlets have traditionally faced less pressure than local news outlets in Hong Kong. After Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020, two local news outlets known for critical coverage of the government, Apple Daily and Stand News, were forced to shut down following the arrest of their senior management. Jimmy Lai, the 78-year-old founder of Apple Daily, was sentenced to 20 years in prison in February. His staffers received prison terms ranging from six years and nine months, to 10 years. Hong Kong, a former British colony that returned to Chinese rule in 1997, ranked 140th out of 180 countries and territories in Reporters Without Borders’ latest World Press Freedom Index, down from 18th out of 139 regions in 2002.

articles.title: US states sue Trump administration, accuse it of ‘illegally’ weakening wildlife law
articles.summary: US News: Twenty US states and Washington, DC, sued US President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday, challenging new rules that they say weaken the fede.
articles.body: Twenty US states and Washington, DC, sued US President Donald Trump's administration on Wednesday, challenging new rules that they say weaken the federal Endangered Species Act. They said that the rules could allow development, mining and oil drilling in habitats of threatened wildlife.The lawsuits, led by Washington state, California, Maryland and Massachusetts, were filed in federal courts in the San Francisco area. They target rules issued by the interior and commerce departments less than two months ago that changed how the landmark 1973 law protects endangered species and their habitats.One lawsuit challenges a new definition of "harm" under the Endangered Species Act. The states say the change removes long-standing protections for wildlife habitats by allowing activities such as oil drilling and mining as long as they are not "directed immediately and intentionally" against particular animals, even if they result in injury or death.The states called the change a "reversal of staggering proportions". They argue that the rules are "arbitrary and capricious" and violate the National Environmental Policy Act.The second lawsuit challenges two other changes. One removes broad protections for species newly classified as threatened unless the US Fish and Wildlife Service introduces protections specifically for that species. The other requires the government to consider objections from businesses, including potential economic costs, before designating areas as "critical habitats".Washington attorney general Nick Brown said the administration was weakening a law that has protected wildlife for decades."The ‌Trump administration is trying to undermine the law, the will of Congress and the will of the people who overwhelmingly support protections ​for endangered species," Washington attorney General ​Nick Brown said at a press conference. "Instead of stewardship, this administration's approach to our land, to our water is one of exploitation."The US interior department rejected the states' claims and said federal agencies should implement the law according to its text."The role of federal agencies is to faithfully implement the Endangered Species Act as written, not to expand its reach through interpretations favoured by advocacy organisations," an Interior Department spokesperson said."This lawsuit seeks to preserve a decades-old regulatory overreach that expanded the Endangered Species Act beyond the authority granted by Congress," the spokesperson added. "The department will vigorously defend its authority to implement the law according to its plain text."The Endangered Species Act, enacted by Congress in 1973, has been credited with helping save species including the California condor, grizzly bear and humpback whale. The states said 99% of the species protected under the law have avoided extinction.Wildlife advocates have long identified habitat loss as a major cause of extinction. New York attorney general Letitia James said the states were seeking to preserve protections for future generations."We owe future generations a world where bald eagles soar, sea turtles ​swim and all wildlife thrives," New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement.The Trump administration has argued that the law has been used to block development projects and impose costs on businesses. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has said the Endangered Species Act has been weaponised to stop projects, hurt competitiveness and undermine national security.Burgum has said the new rules bring the law closer to its original intent.The changes come as the Trump administration seeks to reduce environmental regulations that it says constrain American businesses. The administration has also rolled back several environmental initiatives and reduced support for clean energy.The new rules followed a 2024 US Supreme Court decision that overturned a decades-old precedent requiring courts to defer to federal agencies' reasonable interpretations of laws they administer.The latest lawsuits add to dozens of legal challenges filed by Democratic-led states against major policy changes during Trump's second term. Environmental groups have separately sued to block the revised definition of "harm".Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Before 9/11, families could walk passengers to airport gates; 25 years later a TSA pilot is bringing that back at 13 US airports for PreCheck members
articles.summary: US News: Before 9/11, families could walk passengers to airport gates; 25 years later a TSA pilot is bringing that back at 13 US airports for PreCheck membersP.
articles.body: Before 9/11, families could walk passengers to airport gates; 25 years later a TSA pilot is bringing that back at 13 US airports for PreCheck membersPeople flying through Mesa Gateway Airport in Arizona can now have family members or friends meet them at the gate, even if those visitors are not travelling themselves. According to Fox 10, the airport is among 13 in the US taking part in a pilot programme that allows eligible people to pass through airport security without having a flight ticket.The programme, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck, brings back an experience many American travellers remember from before the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. At that time, people without tickets could travel through the airport and walk with passengers to the gate.That changed after 9/11, when airport security rules became much stricter. Access beyond security checkpoints was generally limited to people with a plane ticket. Now, the pilot programme is testing whether some non-ticketed visitors can once again enter the gate area under existing security rules.Mesa Gateway Airport has been part of the programme for about a week, according to Ryan Smith, the airport's director of communications. "We're only a week into the program," Smith said. "It's been a huge success." The programme gives approved visitors a single-day gate pass, but they must meet certain requirements before they can enter the secure area.How the gate pass worksThe programme is available to people who have TSA PreCheck. Those who want to use it must inform the airport that they want a pass one to three days before the day of the flight.If the request is approved, the visitor receives the gate pass by email. They can then take the pass and their identification to the airport and go through the security checkpoint.Security rules remain in placePeople entering the gate area through the programme are subject to the same security restrictions as ticketed passengers.That security requirement has also been an important part of the discussion around the programme. While many travellers interviewed by FOX 10 said they would welcome the chance to enter the gate area without a ticket, some people said they were concerned about any change to airport security procedures.One traveller said they preferred stronger security measures, even if that meant spending more time going through TSA screening."Oh yeah," the traveller said. "I'm actually scared when they don't find something like hairspray or water in my bottle. I think the more security the better. I mean I don't care how long it takes me to get through TSA."Why travellers want the optionFor many passengers, the biggest benefit is being able to stay with relatives or friends for longer before a flight or meet them immediately after they arrive.People interviewed at Mesa Gateway Airport said the option could be especially useful for families and passengers who need help at the airport.One traveller said the return of gate access would be welcome. "I do miss that a lot," the person said. "That was definitely something to get off the airplane and see somebody right there. I kinda miss doing that."Another person pointed to the needs of older passengers, saying a family member could enter the secure area and help with bags or other needs.The programme could also help families in situations where a child is travelling between divorced parents. One traveller explained that allowing a parent to walk a child all the way to the gate could prevent the child from having to continue alone after passing through security.Another example involved a traveller with autism. "We had a traveler that has a son that's on the spectrum, and they just wanted to go through the process and kind of get used to going through the airport prior to having that ticket booked," the traveller said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: RNLI reviews security after protests in Dover and Portsmouth
articles.summary: Volunteers were targeted online after it assisted in the rescue of people crossing the Channel on Sunday.
articles.body:
The RNLI is reviewing its security procedures to ensure the safety of its members after protests in Dover and Portsmouth which saw its members targeted.

As part of this, volunteers have been told to consider not wearing RNLI branded clothing in some circumstances while representing the charity.

It comes after the charity helped carry around 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight, to Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, where roads were blocked by protesters.

Following this, some crew members had their photos and names shared on social media, in posts accusing them of treason. RNLI chief executive Peter Sparkes called the abuse "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".

In a message sent to volunteers, Sparkes said its participation in the rescue on Sunday had been requested by HM Coastguard.

"This was the first time we have been involved in a Channel crossing incident of this magnitude this far west," he said.

Initially crews from Bembridge and Yarmouth stations were involved, later being joined by crews from four more stations after "large numbers of protesters were in and near the water in Portsmouth".

During the incident, the RNLI said it also helped to ensure the safety of anti-migrant protesters in the sea off Portsmouth.

BBC Verify spoke to Neil, one of the volunteers who was called a "traitor" and whose image was shared online .

"We were there, purely for the safety of the protesters in the water," he said.

"It would be nice for those people who called me a traitor to know that I'm not a traitor."

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, RNLI vice-president Sir Robin Knox-Johnston encouraged people abusing lifeboat crews to "have some sense about this".

Sir Robin, a legendary sailor who was the first man to sail solo non-stop around the world, said: "The people who are abusing the volunteers - I wonder how abusive they'd be if they suddenly got a stitch when they're out swimming?

"They'd be screaming for the RNLI to rescue them and the RNLI would do it."

In his message to volunteers, Peter Sparkes said "at times of increased media activity like this it is only natural that members of the public, supporters, family and friends may have questions about our lifesaving work in the Channel".

"When our crews are tasked by HM Coastguard, we will go to the aid of those who need our assistance, including those crossing one of the world's busiest shipping lanes in small, overcrowded and unseaworthy boats," he said.

"When called upon, we rescue people - men, women, and children - in distress."

He said the the RNLI would then pass over responsibility for the people it rescued to the ambulance service, HM Coastguard, police or Border Force.

Figures from the RNLI show only a tiny fraction of its lifeboat launches involved assisting people "in distress in the Channel", with the majority of small boats intercepted by Border Force.

Sparkes encouraged crew members to take measures to ensure they feel safe in their roles.

He said volunteers could do things like "choosing not to wear RNLI branded clothing when representing our charity in public places" or removing yourself from "removing yourself from a conversation with a member of public if you feel uncomfortable".

He also encouraged RNLI members to visibly wear ID identifying themselves while on site, and to challenge anyone not wearing an ID - especially if they are acting suspiciously or trying to gain access to the building.
